input.question: How allergy shots work.
input.ground_truth: They inject you with a *really tiny* amount of the allergen at first, then subsequent shots up the dosage a little bit at a time. It exposes your body to the allergen in such a way that it never freaks out and eventually realizes that there isn't actually a threat.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: How allergy shots work.

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine your body has tiny guards called "soldiers" that help keep you safe from things that can make you sick, like germs. But sometimes, these soldiers get confused and think something harmless, like a cat or pollen, is a bad guy. That’s what happens when someone has allergies—the soldiers get too excited and cause sneezing, itching, or a runny nose.

Now, allergy shots are like giving your body a tiny bit of that "not-so-bad guy" (like cat hair or pollen) but in a very safe way. You get these shots little by little, and each time, you give your body a chance to learn that this thing isn’t really dangerous. So, over time, your body’s soldiers learn not to get so excited, and they stop causing all the sneezing and itching. That’s how allergy shots help people feel better!
